deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page: no formulas, computations or derivations. It is a continuous prose draft of Riemann's natural-philosophical fragments in the Fechner / 'Psychologie und Metaphysik' complex. Its argument runs as follows.

(A) End of a section on the 'Seelenleben der Erde' (soul-life of the Earth), continuing from the previous page.
- The previous page posited that the ponderable masses inside the solidified crust carry the Earth's psychic life. It then listed empirical conditions of life: 1. protection from external disturbances; 2. physical processes such as absorption, endosmosis, chemical combination and decomposition, and galvanic currents; 3. moist, non-crystalline substances; 4. only the four 'organic' elements serve as general carriers of life; 5. upper and lower temperature limits.
- This page concedes that some of these listed facts seem to refute the hypothesis. They would do so only if the conditions were absolutely valid rather than valid relative to our range of experience.
- Against absolute validity Riemann gives two reasons:
  1. All of nature except the Earth's surface would then be dead, since the temperatures and pressures on other celestial bodies do not allow organic compounds to exist.
  2. It is absurd that organic matter arose from inorganic matter on a lifeless crust. Explaining the first organisms already requires an organising principle, i.e. a life process under conditions where organic compounds could not exist.
- Conclusion: the conditions hold only for life under present surface conditions. If we can explain them, we can judge whether life is possible under other conditions.
- Why are only the four organic elements (C, H, O, N) general carriers of life? Two shared properties are offered:
  1. They and their compounds are the hardest of all substances to condense, some not yet condensable at all (the 'permanent gases').
  2. Their compounds are very diverse and easily decomposed. Riemann notes this could be a consequence rather than a cause of their use in life.
- He argues the first property is the relevant one. This should become clear once conditions of life are derived from facts 2 and 3, and once the phenomena of gases condensing into liquids and solids are traced to their causes. The text breaks off with '...'.

(B) Section II (a heading, struck out, reading roughly 'Psychologie / Metaphysik').
- A review-style appreciation of Fechner's Zend-Avesta as a 'lebendig machendes Wort' (life-giving word), with a footnote: Vgl. Fechner, Zend-Avesta I, Vorrede S. V.
- Old ideas are revived in new form. Life, previously recognised only on the Earth's surface, now appears all around. What was once left to the play of finely working forces now appears as the workshop of the highest mental activity. Riemann says this fulfils what 'our great poet' (presumably Goethe) envisioned.
- On Fechner's method: just as Nanna argued for the ensoulment of plants, Zend-Avesta starts from the ensoulment of the stars.
- The method is not induction of general laws followed by application and testing in explaining nature. It is analogy: the Earth is compared to our own body, which we know to be ensouled. Fechner seeks not only the similarities... (the text continues on the next page).
errors: No mathematical errors are possible, since there is no mathematics on the page.

Scientific content judged by 1850s knowledge: the claim that the organic elements and their compounds are the hardest to condense is broadly right for H2, N2 and O2 and some carbon compounds (CO, CH4), which were 'permanent gases' until 1877 (Cailletet, Pictet). It does not hold for carbon itself or for many organic compounds, and it ignores helium and the noble gases, which were then unknown.
The claim that no other celestial body allows organic compounds to exist is an over-generalisation, even by contemporary standards (Mars was already discussed).
Argument 2 (that abiogenesis on a lifeless crust is absurd) reflects contemporary vitalist or idealist premises and is not a proof.

results.what: Speculative argument that the empirical conditions of life are only relative to present terrestrial surface conditions, and that the organic elements are privileged by their difficult condensability (permanent gases).
results.modern_name: Natural philosophy / panpsychist speculation in the manner of Fechner; no modern scientific equivalent
results.usually_credited_to: Fechner (Zend-Avesta, 1851) for the ensouled Earth; the Riemann fragments themselves were published by Dedekind and Weber (1876, 'Fragmente philosophischen Inhalts')

results.what: Critical review of Fechner's Zend-Avesta and his method of analogy as opposed to induction
results.modern_name: Riemann's philosophical fragments on Fechner (Zur Psychologie und Metaphysik)

deep.surprise_reason: This is purely philosophical and speculative prose. Riemann's engagement with Fechner, including the Zend-Avesta review and the speculations on the Earth's soul-life, is known and largely published in the 'Fragmente philosophischen Inhalts' of the Gesammelte Werke. There is no mathematical content.
transcription_corrections: A page number '4' appears at the top left of the image.
Line 2: 'erscheinend dessen Annahme' is probably 'erscheinen diese Annahme' (these facts appear to refute this assumption).
Item 2: 'auf der unbelebten Erdrinde' fits the image; the sense is 'it is absurd to assume that organic matter arose from inorganic matter on the lifeless crust.'
'Was man erst den Sitz feiner und künstlicher wirkender Kräfte überlassen' is probably 'Was man erst dem Spiel feiner (und) kunstvoll wirkender Kräfte überlassen'; uncertain.
'nur durch Ueberlieferung in das Fortdauernde' is likely 'nur durch Ueberlieferung ... fortdauernd'; reading uncertain.
The red pencil note after the section break is likely an editorial or archival remark (e.g. '(größerer Zwischenraum)'), not Riemann's text.
The struck-out heading after 'II' appears as 'Psychologie [und] Metaphysik' (crossed out), consistent with the published fragment title.
The red note at the footnote ('Siehe Ende der Seite/Zeile') is an archival or editorial addition.
